analysis: This is the best sterling proposition in the sale. William Cripps was a first-rank London silversmith working from the 1740s into the 1760s, and the photographs show a proper period baluster mug -- swelling body, moulded spreading foot, double-scroll handle with a leaf-capped upper terminal. It is comfortably antique, it is a documented named maker, and unlike almost everything else in the silver sections the melt floor sits close underneath the estimate rather than far below it. A pint mug of this form runs 10 to 14 troy ounces, which is roughly $460 to $650 of sterling at the working spot before a refiner's cut.
problems: Called a tankard but shown with no lid, so it is a mug -- do not pay tankard money. The surface carries heavy directional polishing scratches, which on Georgian silver often means a crest or armorial has been buffed out; that thins the body and is the one condition problem that genuinely matters. Check the hallmarks are crisp rather than worn soft, check for a repaired handle joint at the lower terminal, and hold it up to the light for thin spots.
patience: Low to moderate. Georgian mugs by documented makers do appear, but rarely at an estimate this close to their own metal value.
sources: Weight range is a form-based estimate, not a catalogued figure -- confirm on the scale at preview.

analysis: A George III sterling skewer at a $100-200 estimate is the cheapest genuine Georgian silver in the sale. Skewers are unglamorous, which is exactly why they are cheap -- nobody in the room wants one, and the same object with a shell terminal and a good maker's mark would be triple this if it were a spoon.
problems: There is not much metal in a skewer, typically 2 to 3 troy ounces, so about $90-140 of silver. That means at the low estimate you are buying at roughly melt and at the high estimate slightly above it. Check the ring terminal is not split and the hallmarks are legible -- worn marks on a plain object leave you with anonymous silver.
patience: Moderate. Georgian skewers are common but this price is at the bottom of the range.

analysis: Ebenezer Noyes Moulton was a Newburyport and Boston silversmith of the Federal period, part of the Moulton dynasty that is the best-documented family of American silversmiths. A coin silver ladle by a named New England maker is a clean hit on three criteria at once and $300-400 is a fair rather than a bargain price -- but fair for something genuinely good is the right trade for a collection.
problems: Ladles are prone to bowl thinning at the lip and to handle repairs at the junction, which is where they always break. Check for solder colour differences at that joint. A monogram is likely and should not put you off. Weigh it: a substantial ladle is 3 to 5 troy ounces of coin silver, roughly $130-220 of metal, so most of the price is maker premium.
patience: Low to moderate. Named Federal New England silversmiths in this price band are the exact intersection this buyer wants and they are not weekly occurrences.

analysis: Six coin silver spoons by Nehemiah Dodge of Providence, catalogued to circa 1800. Dodge is a documented early Republic maker and six matching spoons is a usable set rather than a fragment. This is precisely the category -- antique, precious metal, named maker, unfashionable enough to be cheap -- where the budget buys something real.
problems: Weigh them; six teaspoons is around 3 to 4 troy ounces of coin silver, so $130-175 of metal against a $300-400 estimate. Check that all six carry the same mark rather than being a made-up set, and look at the bowl tips for the wear that comes from two centuries of stirring.
patience: Moderate. Coin silver spoons are everywhere; matched named-maker sets of six with a date attribution are less common.

analysis: Twelve American coin silver teaspoons, mid-19th century. The same logic as the Dodge spoons but larger and without the named maker -- which is why it is the same estimate for twice the metal. If you want the silver rather than the signature, this is the better buy of the two.
problems: Mixed makers are likely in a group of twelve; check whether it is actually a matched set or an accumulation. At roughly 6 to 8 troy ounces the metal is $260-350, so the $300-500 estimate is at melt on the low end -- which makes the low end a genuinely good buy and the high end unremarkable.
patience: High. Coin silver spoon groups run constantly.

analysis: Twelve 19th-century British sterling teaspoons at $300-500. British sterling is 92.5% against coin silver's 90%, so marginally better metal, and the hallmarks make dating unambiguous rather than inferred.
problems: This is a melt-adjacent lot and the estimate sits above melt. Twelve teaspoons is about 6 to 7 troy ounces, so roughly $280-325 of sterling and $240-290 after a refiner. Buy at the low estimate or below; there is no maker premium being offered here.
patience: Very high. English sterling flatware is the most consistently available precious metal at any general sale.

analysis: Eight English sterling teaspoons at a $200-300 estimate -- the smaller and cheaper of the two English spoon lots, and proportionally the better value if it goes at the low end. Around 4 to 5 troy ounces, so $185-230 of metal.
problems: At $200 you are buying at melt; at $300 you are paying a 30% premium for nothing in particular. Discipline matters more than analysis on lots like this. Check for a matched set rather than assembled odds.
patience: Very high.

analysis: An 18th-century pine sea chest at $300-500 is the best value-per-criterion lot in Day 2. It is catalogued to the 18th century, so the house has committed; it is a genuine maritime object rather than a decorative one; and sea chests are the furniture form most closely tied to the coastal Maine story. At this estimate it is cheaper than most reproduction blanket chests.
problems: Check the construction before the paint: hand-cut dovetails with visible scribe lines, irregular pit-saw or up-and-down saw marks on the interior, and shrinkage that has pulled the boards out of square all confirm the date. Circular saw marks anywhere mean it is not 18th century. Original becket handles are usually gone; replaced rope beckets are acceptable and normal. Look for a fitted till and for old, dry paint rather than a decorative repaint.
patience: Moderate. Sea chests are common in Maine but 18th-century examples at this money are not.

analysis: The 19th-century companion to lot 2068 at the same estimate. A century younger and correspondingly more common, but still a genuine period sea chest at $300-500 and still comfortably over the antique line.
problems: The same construction checks apply, and on a 19th-century chest circular saw marks are expected rather than disqualifying, so the dating rests more on the joinery and the paint. Beware of decorated chests where the painted ship or name is a recent addition -- that is a well-established trade.
patience: High. 19th-century sea chests appear at most Maine sales.

analysis: The description turns this from a good instrument into a documented one. A mid-19th-century English marine sextant by SPENCER, BROWNING & CO., London -- one of the great names in navigational instruments -- retailed by S. THAXTER & SON, BOSTON, in ebony and brass with a bone-inlaid arc and maker's plaque, with a DATE OF 1870 STAMPED TO THE BACK OF THE FRAME, and 'originally the property of Captain Ebenezer Palmer, Dorchester'. That is a named maker, a named American retailer, a stamped year and a named owning captain on one object. For a coastal Maine collection this is the marine criterion and the antique criterion met together with documentation, and at $500-700 it is inside the band.
problems: 'Split to top of case' -- the case is original and a split lid is a repair, not a disaster, but it is the one stated fault. Completeness is still the question the catalogue does not answer: count the telescopes, the shades and the key against the fitted recesses, because a sextant missing its inverting scope or its shades is worth a fraction. The Palmer provenance is asserted, not evidenced; ask what it rests on. 'Dorchester, N.P.' is unexplained -- the catalogue guesses New Brunswick, which would make him a Maritimes rather than a Massachusetts captain.
patience: Moderate. Sextants run regularly in marine sales; complete cased examples by top makers less so.

analysis: A circa-1910 model of the sailing ship L.F. Chase of Rockland, Maine is exactly what the brief means by hyper-local material with a small but committed regional audience. It names a specific midcoast port twelve miles from Thomaston and a specific identified vessel, and it is catalogued to a date that sits right on the antique line. Named-vessel Maine models do not come round often.
problems: Sits on the 1926 line rather than safely behind it, so treat the age claim as borderline rather than settled. Models suffer -- check the rigging is original rather than restrung, that no spars are replaced, and whether the case is period. A model that has been restored is a decorative object; one with its original dusty rigging intact is a document.
patience: Low. Identified midcoast vessels are the honest case for going past comp.

analysis: Maine redware attributed to Matthias Norcross is genuinely scarce material. Maine had comparatively few potteries and their output is thinly represented in collections, so attributed pieces carry real interest with the New England redware collectors and with the state historical market simultaneously. At $500-700 this is fairly priced for something that is both antique and locally significant.
problems: Attributed is the word to watch -- it is an argument, not a fact, and Maine redware attributions are often made on regional characteristics rather than a mark. Ask what the attribution rests on. Redware is soft and chips readily; check the rim and base for losses and for restoration, which is common and often well hidden under paint.
patience: Low. Attributed Maine redware is uncommon enough that this is a legitimate stretch.

analysis: A grain-painted stand signed or attributed to C.F. Hopf of Kennebunk, Maine at $300-400 is the sort of lot this brief was written to find. Maine-made painted furniture with a named town is doubly documented, grain painting is the decorative surface the folk-art market actually pays for, and the estimate is a fraction of what the same object makes when a Portland dealer describes it properly.
problems: Original grain paint versus later decoration is the entire value question. Period graining shows through-wear on the top and edges, has settled into an even mellow tone, and the paint has cracked with the wood rather than over it. Check the top is original to the base and that the stand has not been reduced in height, which is common.
patience: Low. Named-maker Maine painted furniture at this price is genuinely uncommon.

analysis: A Queen Anne tiger maple tilt-top candlestand catalogued to the period at $500-700. Compare this directly with lot 1017 on Day 1, which is the same form with no date claim at $300-400 -- here the house has committed to the period and the timber is figured, which is where the value difference lies.
problems: Tiger maple is also the timber most often used for Colonial Revival reproductions precisely because it looks expensive. Check the underside for hand-planing and irregular saw marks, the birdcage for hand-cut wedges, and the top for the slight out-of-round that two centuries of shrinkage produces. A perfectly circular top is a warning.
patience: Moderate. Period candlestands appear regularly but tiger maple examples with a period attribution are the better end.

analysis: The second Queen Anne tiger maple candlestand in the same consignment, estimated $300-500 against 2122's $500-700. Two comparable stands in one sale is the classic setup where the second one goes cheap because the people who wanted a candlestand already bought one.
problems: Same construction checks as 2122. The lower estimate presumably reflects a plainer top or a condition issue -- establish which at preview, because a lesser example at a lower price is still a good buy while a damaged one is not.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: A red-painted 18th-century ladderback armchair at $500-700 is a genuine period country chair with the surface that collectors want. Original red paint on 18th-century New England seating is the single most sought-after surface in American country furniture.
problems: Establish that the red is original and not a 20th-century Colonial Revival repaint -- period red is thin, worn through on the arms and front stretcher, and darker in the crevices. Check the feet for height loss, which is universal and forgivable up to a point, and whether the rush or splint seat is original or replaced. A replaced seat is normal.
patience: Moderate. Painted 18th-century chairs appear regularly in New England but original-surface examples at this price are the better end of the range.

analysis: A carved oak bible box catalogued to the 17th century at $500-700 is remarkable value in absolute terms -- this is an object older than almost anything else in the sale, and the price is that of a middling piece of Victoriana. Bible boxes are the entry point into genuine 17th-century oak and they are portable, useful and durable in a way that most early furniture is not.
problems: The category is heavily faked and, more often, heavily improved: plain period boxes are carved later to raise their value. Look at the carving's wear pattern -- period carving is worn smooth on the high points and dirty in the recesses, later carving is crisp and clean-cut with bright wood in the grounds. Check for a replaced lid and modern hinges, both of which are near-universal and only moderately damaging.
patience: Low to moderate. Genuine 17th-century oak at this money is uncommon and the price band is unlikely to hold.

analysis: An oak bible box carrying a carved date of 1681 at $400-600. A dated example is more interesting than an undated one and the date is the house's stated claim, but the date is also the first thing a later improver would add.
problems: Test the date the same way as the carving on 2295: a period-cut date has the same wear, colour and tool character as the surrounding surface. A date cut later reads brighter and sharper than everything around it. Given the price difference against 2295, ask why the dated box is cheaper -- that usually means the house is less confident.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: An 18th-century pine bible box at $400-600 -- the plainer, later and cheaper member of the bible-box group. Pine rather than oak, so less desirable to the English-oak collectors, but a straightforward period object.
problems: Pine boxes are simple enough that reproduction is easy and undetectable from photographs. The construction tells: hand-cut dovetails, rosehead nails, and interior surfaces that have oxidised to a deep brown rather than being merely stained. Check for a replaced bottom.
patience: High. Pine boxes are common.

analysis: A large 18th-century oak bible box at $500-700, the fourth in the group. Four comparable boxes in one sale is a consignment, and consignments of near-identical objects reliably exhaust their buyers -- the last one to cross the block usually goes cheapest. Watch all four and bid the one the room has tired of.
problems: Large is a mixed blessing: bigger boxes were more often converted to other uses and more often lost their lids. Same carving and construction checks as the others.
patience: Moderate, and improved by the fact that you have four chances at essentially the same object in one afternoon.

analysis: A 16th-century oak child's chair at $400-600 is either the most remarkable value in the entire sale or it is not what the catalogue says. Genuine 16th-century seating furniture of any kind is museum material; a child's chair from that date surviving in usable condition would normally carry four figures at minimum. Seven photographs suggests the house is showing it thoroughly, which is a good sign.
problems: The estimate is the problem. When a house catalogues something to the 16th century and then estimates it at $400, the estimate is telling you what the specialists actually think. Assume heavy restoration, substantial replacement, or a much later date -- 17th or 18th century oak is routinely optimistically catalogued. Examine the joints for replaced pegs, the seat for renewal, and the overall surface for the deep, hard, almost black patina that genuinely early oak develops.
patience: Low if genuine, irrelevant if not. Worth the preview trip to resolve.

analysis: A 1652 edition of Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy at $500-700. This is a 17th-century book of genuine literary standing -- one of the monuments of English prose -- at a price that reflects the fact that most auction rooms do not have a rare-book bidder in them. Comfortably antique by nearly three centuries, and unlike most objects in this sale it will still be exactly what it is in another three.
problems: Condition dominates early book values. Check the collation for completeness, particularly the engraved title page, which is the leaf most often missing or supplied in facsimile. Look at the binding -- a period calf binding, even worn, is far preferable to a 19th-century rebind. Damp-staining and worming are usual; loose or detached boards are common and repairable.
patience: Low to moderate. Genuine 17th-century imprints at this money are not a regular occurrence at a Maine general sale.

analysis: An 1837 edition of Bowditch's New American Practical Navigator at $200-300 is the single cheapest genuine antique in the marine section. Bowditch is the foundational American navigation text, this is an early edition dated a century and a half before the antique line, and the New England maritime connection is direct. It is the kind of object that does exactly what the brief asks: if you ever had to let it go, you lose very little.
problems: Early Bowditch editions were working books carried at sea and they show it -- water damage, salt staining, loose signatures and missing plates or tables are all common. Check the plates and folding charts are present, since those are what get removed. A shaken but complete copy is a much better buy than a pretty incomplete one.
patience: Moderate. Bowditch editions appear regularly but pre-1840 ones in a marine sale usually attract more than this.

analysis: An 1820-1830 New Bedford whaler's trying house accounts ledger at $500-700 is a primary document of the American whale fishery, dated to a decade and tied to the industry's principal port. Manuscript business records from the whaling trade are genuinely scarce -- most were pulped -- and they connect directly to the marine and whaling material this buyer is looking at across the day.
problems: Ledgers are bulky and their value depends on legibility and on how much is actually written in. Check the proportion of used pages and whether the hand is readable. Damp damage to the lower edges is near-universal on maritime paper. This is a document to read, not to display, so be honest about whether that is what you want.
patience: Low. Dated whaling manuscript records are uncommon.

analysis: Twelve early 19th-century American ship and private passports at $400-600 -- roughly $40 a document for signed period maritime paper. Ship's passports carry engraved vignettes, official seals and sometimes presidential or cabinet signatures, and twelve of them gives you the option to keep the best and pass the rest along.
problems: Condition varies enormously within groups like this and the photographs show only two views. Expect folds, seal losses and browning. Check whether any carry notable signatures, which is where a group like this can carry a surprise, and whether the count is actually twelve.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: A large group of pre-1865 maritime ship's papers at $600-800. The catalogue has committed to a date ceiling rather than a range, which is a usefully specific claim, and quantity here is genuine value because individual period ship's papers retail at $40-100 each.
problems: Large group means unsorted, and unsorted means the good pieces may already have been removed. Only two photographs for what is described as a large group is not much disclosure. This lot is worth the preview time to actually go through -- the difference between a box of routine crew lists and one containing a Maine vessel's papers is the whole value.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: Two hand-forged 19th-century whaling harpoon tips at $300-500. Genuine whalecraft is honest, dated, hand-made iron with an unambiguous industrial history, and toggle or single-flue harpoon heads are the most recognisable objects the fishery produced. Forged ironwork of this kind is also almost impossible to fake convincingly at this price point.
problems: Check for maker's stamps, which raise the interest substantially -- New Bedford and Fairhaven smiths marked their work. Distinguish genuine period pieces from the decorative reproductions made for the tourist trade from the 1950s onward: period heads show hammer facets, an irregular weld line at the socket, and deep even pitting rather than a uniform rusted surface.
patience: Moderate. Whalecraft runs regularly in marine sales but marked examples are the better end.

analysis: A heart-shaped whaling blubber spade at $300-400, catalogued 19th century and described as rare. The heart-shaped form is a distinctive and less common variant of the cutting spade, and blubber spades display well because the blade shape is immediately legible as what it is.
problems: Rare is the auctioneer's adjective and should be discounted accordingly. The handle is almost certainly replaced -- original hafts rarely survive -- which is acceptable but should not be paid for. Check the blade for cracks at the socket.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: A forged iron flensing tool at $200-300 is the cheapest genuine 19th-century whalecraft in the sale. Same category as the harpoons and spade, at the bottom of the price range because the form is less immediately decorative.
problems: Less decorative also means harder to display and harder to sell on. Check for a maker's stamp, which is what would lift it above the general run.
patience: High. Long whaling tools are the commonest whalecraft category.

analysis: A 19th-century English brass telescope by J.P. Cutts, Sutton & Son of Sheffield at $300-500. Cutts was a substantial optical maker and the signature is a genuine attribution. There are five or six telescopes scattered through Day 2 and this is the one with a documented maker at a sensible price.
problems: Check the optics actually resolve -- delaminated or fungused lenses are common and effectively unrepairable at this value. Check the draw tubes slide without binding and that the lens caps and sunshade are present. Dents in the brass barrel are cosmetic; a bent draw is not.
patience: Moderate. Telescopes are common in marine sales, signed ones by known makers less so.

analysis: A Victorian ship's-wheel-form aneroid barometer at $300-500 is a decorative marine instrument in a popular novelty form. Genuinely Victorian by the catalogue's claim, and barometers hang well.
problems: The ship's wheel form was reproduced heavily from the 1920s through the 1970s for the nautical decor trade, so the Victorian claim needs testing -- period examples have a hand-painted dial, a properly signed movement and heavier turned spokes. Aneroid movements of this age rarely work accurately and repair is uneconomic.
patience: High. Nautical barometers of this type are a decorating staple with deep supply.

analysis: A punched tin lantern with exterior candle at $200-300. The form is right for the first half of the 19th century and these are pleasant, honest objects, but the catalogue makes no date claim at all.
problems: Punched tin lanterns are among the most reproduced of all American country objects -- the Colonial Revival made them by the thousand and craft reproductions continue today. Period tin shows uneven hand-cut seams, soft irregular punching, and rust that has eaten through from the inside. Bright, evenly punched tin with a clean base is modern.
patience: Very high.

analysis: Eight carved wooden butter stamps, catalogued 19th century, at $300-500. Butter prints are genuine folk carving, individually cheap but interesting in quantity, and eight gives a range of motifs. The bidding has already started at $175, which is higher than most lots in this band and suggests someone has noticed.
problems: Reproduction butter stamps exist but are usually obvious -- period examples show deep grease staining in the carving, worn handles, and hairline shrinkage cracks radiating from the centre. Check that all eight are period rather than a mixed group with fillers.
patience: Moderate. Butter stamps are common individually; groups of eight less so.

analysis: A 19th-century painted wooden checkerboard at $200-300. Period game boards are a well-established folk art category, they hang as graphic objects, and this is at the cheap end of the range because it is described plainly rather than as folk art.
problems: Game boards are extensively faked because the formula is simple and the market rewards good paint. Period boards show paint that has worn through where pieces were slid, a board that has warped and split with age, and colours that have gone dull rather than staying crisp. Check the reverse -- fakers finish the front and neglect the back.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: A 19th-century needlework sampler at $300-500, unattributed and undated within the century, sitting alongside two much more expensive samplers in the same section. The cheap one in a group of three is often the best value if condition is sound.
problems: Samplers live or die on the inscription: a signed and dated example with a place name is worth several times an anonymous one, which is presumably why this is the cheap lot. Check for fading -- most samplers have lost their original colour on the exposed face -- and for a modern remount that has trimmed the edges.
patience: High. Samplers are a steady category with regular supply.

analysis: Seven 18th-century English pewter plates at $200-300 -- about $35 a plate for genuinely 18th-century metalwork. Pewter has no melt floor worth speaking of, so this is bought purely as period tableware, but the date is unambiguous and the price is low.
problems: Pewter is soft and 18th-century plates are usually scratched, knife-cut and dented; that is normal wear rather than damage. Check for touch marks on the reverse, which is what distinguishes a documented piece from anonymous metal, and for the pitting and grey scale that indicates tin pest, which is not recoverable.
patience: High. Pewter is a soft market with plenty of supply.

analysis: An 18th-century pewter charger with an engraved heraldic crest at $300-500. The crest lifts it above the plain plates -- engraved armorials on pewter are less common and give the piece a specific history if the arms can be identified.
problems: Engraved crests were also added later to plain pewter to make it saleable, a practice going back to the 19th century. Period engraving is worn in sympathy with the surrounding surface. Also note the brief's standing point about monograms: the market discounts them, which here works in your favour.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: Nine 19th-century pewter measures at $500-700. Graduated sets of measures display well as a group, which is most of what they have going for them, and nine is a substantial run.
problems: Only one photograph for nine objects is thin disclosure. Measures are usually heavily dented at the rim and lip. Check whether the set is actually graduated and complete or an assembled group of odd sizes, which is far more common and much less interesting.
patience: High.

analysis: Two original drawings by John Leech at $300-400. Leech was Punch's principal cartoonist and the original illustrator of Dickens's A Christmas Carol -- a properly documented Victorian name, and original drawings rather than prints. Original works on paper by a listed 19th-century illustrator at $150 each is genuine value.
problems: Confirm they are original drawings and not proof impressions or photomechanical facsimiles -- pencil and ink on paper shows pressure and correction, print does not. Leech's work is signed with initials or a monogram rather than a full signature, so an unsigned sheet needs the attribution explained.
patience: Moderate. Original Victorian illustration drawings appear periodically and are consistently underpriced relative to the artists' reputations.

analysis: An early 18th-century British bird's-eye estate print at $300-500. Kip and Knyff style estate views are handsome graphic objects, genuinely of the period, and they carry the topographical interest that keeps them saleable.
problems: These plates were reprinted through the 19th century and reproduced in the 20th. Check for a plate mark, laid paper with chain lines, and the slightly uneven inking of a hand-pulled impression. Trimmed margins are the usual condition failing and they matter here because the engraved title and key are in the margin.
patience: Moderate.

analysis: A cased 19th-century French ivory and silver coin purse at $200-300 is a genuinely antique small object at a modest price, and in isolation it would be a reasonable BUY IF CHEAP.
problems: It carries the ivory complication for very little compensating value -- there is negligible silver content, no named maker and no particular rarity. Elephant ivory is restricted for interstate commerce under the Endangered Species Act and documentation is unlikely to accompany a $250 lot. On something this modest the constraint outweighs the object. The same reasoning applies across the sale's substantial ivory content -- see the sale-wide note.
patience: Irrelevant.

analysis: A mahogany-cased double sailor's valentine is a genuinely desirable form and this one is estimated $2,000-3,000 with a $1,000 opening -- comprehensively outside the budget band. Noted here rather than screened silently because it is the sort of lot that draws attention away from the affordable marine material.
problems: Beyond the price, sailor's valentines are among the most reproduced maritime objects -- Barbados workshops have made them continuously since the 19th century and modern examples are made specifically for the antique trade. At this money authentication would matter enormously.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band.

analysis: A Simmons eagle sternboard from Rockland, Maine is the single most on-brief object in Day 2 -- carved Maine maritime folk art, named town, named carver. It is also estimated $3,000-5,000 with a $1,500 opening, which is three to five times the budget ceiling.
problems: Worth knowing about and worth seeing at preview for the education, but bidding on it would mean abandoning the budget discipline that makes the rest of this list work. Flagged so it is a deliberate decision rather than a surprise on the day.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band.
